To: group:levy-longsight-noticeboard
Replying to: none
Cc: none
Subject: Please read and share: fake tablets and when to call 999

Parents, teenagers, anyone who might be out with their mates — please take a minute to read this. The police warning is already on here, but it needs to reach people, not get lost down the page.

Blue tablets being sold as diazepam or “Xanax” have been found to contain nitazenes. These are synthetic opioids that can be far stronger than heroin. You cannot tell what’s in a tablet by looking at it, or because someone says it’s the same stuff they’ve had before.

I’m an ICU nurse and a mum. This is general safety advice, not a comment on Saturday or confirmation of anything being said about it. I’m not sharing any information about patients. Please don’t put names or guesses in the comments either.

If someone has taken something and becomes unwell, ring 999 straight away. If they collapse, are very drowsy or difficult to wake, have slow or noisy breathing, or their lips look blue, it is an emergency. Pinpoint pupils — the black centres of the eyes looking unusually tiny — can also be a warning sign. You do not need to see every sign before calling.

Do not put them to bed to “sleep it off”. Do not leave them alone. Someone who looks asleep or sounds like they’re snoring may not be breathing properly. Waiting can mean their brain is going without enough oxygen, and that can cause permanent injury or death.

Tell the 999 call handler where you are, what’s happening and what you think they’ve taken, if you know. Follow their instructions. If they’re not breathing normally, they can talk you through CPR. If they’re unconscious but breathing normally, put them in the recovery position and keep checking their breathing while help comes.

To the young people reading this: please don’t spend time worrying about whether your parents will find out or whether you’ll get into trouble. Get help first. You don’t have to know exactly what your mate took, and you don’t have to handle it on your own.

The police have explicitly said: “Our priority is preserving life.” That matters. Please make sure your kids hear it.

Nasal naloxone can reverse an opioid overdose, including one caused by nitazenes. It does not replace an ambulance: ring 999, use it if available and follow the instructions. More doses may be needed, and someone can become unwell again after it wears off.

Brightpath drug & alcohol service on Stockport Road, next to the launderette, has free nasal naloxone kits. Anyone can ask, no names needed. Training takes about 10 minutes. They’re open Monday–Friday, 10–4, and until 7 on Thursdays. You don’t have to be someone who takes drugs to carry something that could save a life.

I had this chat with my lad, who’s 14, over his tea last night. There were eye rolls. But he listened, and he asked what pinpoint pupils meant. It doesn’t have to be a perfect conversation. Please have it THIS week, not after half term or when you think they’re old enough.

And please stop slagging kids off. Frightened kids who expect a telling-off can be frightened to call for help. We need them to know they can ring immediately, whatever has happened.

Please share this, don’t just like it. Put the police warning in your family chats and make sure your teenagers know: if a mate goes down, ring 999. Don’t wait.
